segments.text: We turn now to Philippians 3.
Finally, my brethren, rejoice in the Lord.
To write the same things again is no trouble to me, and it is a safe God for you.
Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the false
circumcision, for we are the true circumcision who worship in the Spirit of
God, and glory in Christ Jesus, and put no confidence in the flesh.
Here Paul is speaking about the difference between the new covenant's
circumcision and the old covenant's circumcision.
In the old covenant, circumcision was an external thing, an external
cutting off of the flesh from a male child.
In the new covenant, circumcision is an internal thing.
It is a matter of the heart.
And as Paul says elsewhere in Romans 2, we read that the true
circumcision is that which is of the heart, Romans 2.29, and it is by the Spirit, not
by the letter.
And this is what he speaks of here in verse 3.
It is very important for us to see the difference and the distinction between the new
covenant and the old covenant.
In the old covenant, almost everything was external.
The blessings that God promised Israel under the old covenant were external blessings,
riches, property, a physical land on this earth, children, and happy homes and prosperity
in one's fields and cattle, and so many things like that.
Likewise, the law or the old covenant could clean up a man's life only on the
external.
The commandments, the Ten Commandments that God gave, related mostly to the external
aspects of one's life.
The law was powerless when it came to sin in a man's heart.
Couldn't do anything about it and couldn't punish a man if there was sin in his heart.
It is only when that sin came forth externally that it could be punished.
And likewise, the temple was a physical external temple in the old covenant.
And many other things about the old covenant are physical and external, just like
circumcision.
Now, all this is changed in the new covenant to something internal and spiritual.
Now, Paul had already spoken to the Philippians about this.
He says in verse 1, Finally, my brethren, rejoice in the Lord.
And he goes on to speak about joy in chapter 4 as well.
But there can be no pure joy unless we have experienced this spiritual
circumcision in our hearts.
That is why he goes on to speak about this circumcision and all that follows from it
in the remaining verses of chapter 3.
And he says in verse 1, To write the same things again is no trouble to me.
Obviously, he had spoken about these things when he was in Philippi, probably even written
to them earlier.
And he says, Now I am writing the same things again.
The same things as I told you, perhaps, or the same things that I wrote to you earlier.
In any case, he had already told them about these things, about what the true circumcision
was.
But he says, It is no trouble for me to remind you of these things, and it is a safeguard
for you as well.
Now, this is one thing that the apostles were not afraid of doing, of repeating themselves
and keeping on repeating themselves, because they knew, as we know, how poor a memory
we have concerning these things.
Peter says in the second episode of Peter chapter 1 and verse 12, Therefore I shall always
be ready to remind you of these things, even though you already know them, and have been
established in the truth which is present with you.
This is how it was with Peter.
He says, I am always ready to tell you the same things again.
I am not ashamed of it.
It is good for you.
And John says that in 1 John 2 21, I have not written to you because you do not know the
truth, but because you know it.
You already know it, and I am repeating it to you again.
And Jude says in the episode of Jude verse 5, Now I desire to remind you, though you
know all things once for all.
And so we find Paul, Peter, John, Jude, each of them are not afraid of repetition.
They are not afraid of saying the same things because they were not interested, as many
preachers are today, of gaining a reputation for saying something new and clever.
They were more interested in establishing these believers in the faith, and if that required
repetition they were willing to repeat themselves.
And so Paul says in Philippians 3.1, To write the same things again is no trouble to me,
and it is a safe God for you.
Do you realize that when you hear the same word again and again, it is a safe God for
us, it protects us?
Because we so easily forget.
For example, we must have read 1 Thessalonians 5.18 many times, where it says, In everything
give thanks, for this is the will of God concerning you in Christ Jesus.
Now how many people who have read that actually do it?
They need to be reminded again and again and again that we are to give thanks in
everything.
Now that is just one example of how easy it is to forget what the word of God teaches.
Now verse 2 it says, Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the false
circumcision.
Now these are the people who were keen on bringing the believers back under law, and
that is happening even today.
That is back to just concentrating on the external aspects of life, on the external
aspects of purity, and who do not concern themselves so much about the inward.
And here Paul calls them dogs.
Now a dog we read in 2 Peter in chapter 2, and verse 22 is one who returns to his own
vomit.
What he has brought up and thrown out of his system, the dog goes back and eats again.
And what Paul is saying is, if you have thrown out something from your system, you have
thrown out that life where you lived only in the externals, and now you have come
into a life which is far superior to that, because you have come to inward purity,
and you seek for an inward purity.
Now to go back from that, to eat again what you have vomited out, makes you a dog.
What these dogs are doing is seeking to bring people back under law, back under a system
of rules and regulations that would keep them pure on the outside, but would give them
no victory over sin in their hearts.
Now Jesus spoke about dogs in Matthew chapter 7.
He spoke on the Sermon on the Mount, he says in Matthew 7.6,
�Don�t give that which is holy to the dogs.� Now that which is holy, that which
God has given, cannot be appreciated by those who are only interested in an external
life.
If you are interested just in an external testimony that your life is clean and good,
then you cannot understand the new covenant.
And then you will be like a dog.
You will not have victory.
We read in Galatians 5 about one characteristic of dogs, Galatians 5.15.
If you bite and devour one another, that�s what dogs do.
They bite and bark and fight with one another, and where people call themselves
Christians and bite and bark and fight with one another, they are actually dogs.
That�s not the nature of God.
That�s not the divine nature to bite and bark and fight with people.
No, that�s the characteristic of a dog.
That�s the characteristic of those who are unregenerate.
Their lives are not changed, and it is because they have not understood what the true
circumcision is.
And these dogs become evil workers, beware of the dogs, beware of evil workers.
Yet they would be preaching from the Old Testament, but they would be evil workers.
A man can take the Bible and be an evil worker, because he can don�t sin.
Where a person can don�t sin and says, �Well, you have to be defeated.
As long as you live in this world, you have to sin.� What is he doing?
He is not a worker leading people to godliness.
He is an evil worker, beware of the false circumcision, those who speak much about the
externals, but don�t realize that the entire New Covenant leads to the law being written
in our hearts and in our minds.
Now, it is very important for us to see this distinction if we are to enter into the New
Covenant and be protected from those who would seek to bring us back under the law.
It turned out to Philippians 3.
Last week we saw how Paul warned the Philippians to beware of the false circumcision in verse
And then he goes on to say in verse 3 that we are the true circumcision, who worship in
the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh.
And this is the mark of the true circumcision.
The Old Covenant�s circumcision was an external cutting off of the flesh in a male
child.
The true circumcision of which that was only a picture was the putting off of confidence
in the flesh and not walking according to the flesh, the flesh being crucified.
Or we could put it in other words, in the Old Testament temple there was a veil.
We are told in Hebrews 10.20 that the veil is the flesh, the flesh of Jesus, which
is the same flesh as ours.
And this veil was rent when Jesus completed His earthly life and finally died on the cross
of Calvary, because Jesus had completed a work in the flesh, in the flesh of man,
where all sin had been condemned in the flesh.
And the veil which blocked off God from man and prevented man from approaching God
was rent, and the way was opened into the most holy place.
This is another difference between the Law and the Gospel, between the Old
Covenant and the New Covenant.
The Old Covenant could bring a man as far as the holy place of the
tabernacle of the temple, but beyond that lay the veil.
That symbolized the flesh, because of the flesh of man in which there was no
good thing, man could not enter into God�s presence until Jesus came in that
flesh and overcame sin and finally died on the cross, so that now our old man
has been crucified with Jesus.
We can put off the old man by faith and by the power of the Holy Spirit,
mortify the deeds of our body, these deeds that are the result of our having
a flesh in which dwells no good thing.
And so it says in Galatians 5.24 that they that are Christ have crucified
the flesh with its affections and lusts.
That is the true circumcision.
And that is what Paul is speaking of here in verse 3.
We are the true circumcision of which the Old Testament circumcision was only a symbol
and a type.
What it really referred to and pointed to was what we are doing now, that is,
crucifying the flesh and overcoming.
Now we worship in the Spirit of God.
In the Old Testament they could not worship in the Spirit of God because the Holy
Spirit was not yet given to indwell man in that way.
But now the Spirit has been given to indwell man so that man need not worship only with
his body and with his soul, that is, with his intellect and his emotions and his body,
but he can go beyond the soul into the realm of the Spirit, beyond the Holy
Place, through the veil, into the Most Holy, which symbolizes the Spirit.
The Old Testament tabernacle had three parts to it, the outer court, the Holy
Place and the Most Holy Place, that being the dwelling place of God corresponds to man
who is God's dwelling place, being of three parts, as we read in 1 Thessalonians 5.23,
body, soul, and spirit.
And so now we can worship in the Spirit.
In the Old Testament they could worship only with the body and in the soul, because
there was a veil beyond the soul between the Holy Place and the Most Holy.
But now we can worship in the Spirit of God.
Jesus spoke about this in John 4, when he told the woman of Samaria,
the hour is coming and now is when the true worshipers will worship the Father in
Spirit.
Verse 23 and 24.
This was a new day that was dawning, Jesus told the Samaritan woman,
and we could worship God in the Spirit, in intimate communion.
And this is the result of this circumcision, of the flesh, being rent, the veil being
rent.
Now we can worship in the Spirit of God.
The glory that is in the Most Holy Place can flood our whole personality.
And we glory in Christ Jesus, it says in Philippians 3.3.
We have no glory in ourselves.
We recognize that in our flesh dwells no good thing, as we see in Romans 7.18.
And therefore, whatever comes forth from our flesh can never be acceptable to God.
Even the righteousness that comes forth from the flesh is unacceptable to God,
because it is like filthy rags, as we read in Isaiah 64.6.
And so we can glory in nothing.
There's nothing that we can do, unaided by the Holy Spirit, that can ever be
acceptable to God.
There are a lot of good things we could do, but none of them would be acceptable to God
until we have experienced this circumcision.
And once you have experienced this circumcision where we have no more confidence in our flesh,
then we recognize that we cannot offer to God an acceptable service.
No?
And therefore, we come to the place described in Romans 12, verses 1 and 2, that we present
our bodies, not to do this, that, and the other for God.
That's what they did in the Old Testament.
And that's what many people do today who don't have understanding of the New Covenant.
But we are told in Romans 12, verse 1, that we are to present our bodies as a living
sacrifice, that in this body we are to slay, for that's what sacrifice means, slay the
lusts of the flesh.
And we offer this body as a perpetual sacrifice to God.
And this is our spiritual service of worship.
This is the service and worship that is acceptable to God.
And then we cannot glory in it.
All the credit goes to the Lord Jesus Christ.
When we can take credit and glory for something we do, we can say that we haven't
experienced that true circumcision.
But Paul says we are the true circumcision who glory in Christ Jesus.
There's absolutely nothing that I can glory in myself anymore.
And the third thing he says there in verse 3 is that we put no confidence in the flesh.
We have absolutely no confidence in our own abilities.
Now where a man is full of self-sufficiency and confident that he can do something for
God, he has confidence in his flesh.
But the true circumcision are those who worship God in the spirit and who give all the glory
to Christ Jesus and glory only in him, not in what they are and their abilities, and
who have no confidence that their flesh can ever please God in any way.
Now when we come to that place, then we have entered into the New Covenant community
of God's people, the true circumcision.
And just like in the Old Testament, physical circumcision was a mark of God's people.
Here is the mark of God's true people today, Philippians 3.3, the true circumcision.
They worship God in the spirit.
They glory not in themselves or what they are or what they have, but in Christ Jesus.
And they have no confidence in their flesh.
It's good for each one of us to evaluate ourselves in relation to these three things, to see where
we stand.
Do we glory in anything that we have, our appearance or our knowledge or our wisdom or
our wealth or our position?
Then we haven't experienced a thorough circumcision.
Do we have confidence in our own abilities?
Then we haven't experienced a thorough circumcision.
Are we still taken up with worship which is mostly external but not inward and spiritual
primarily?
Then we haven't experienced the true circumcision also.
Now, here are the marks of the true circumcision.
And Paul says, if there is any man who can have confidence in the flesh, I would have
more confidence and more opportunity to have confidence than anybody else.
That's what he says in verse 4, because he says, I had so many good things in my favor.
I was circumcised the eighth day as a good Jew, belonging to the nation of Israel,
God's chosen people, of the tribe of Benjamin, the Hebrew of the Hebrews, and as to the
law of Pharisee.
Those are the people who were very meticulous about the jot and the
tittle of the law, and that's what Paul was, and as to zeal, a persecutor of the
church, and as to the righteousness which is in the law, he was found blameless.
In other words, his external life was also clean and tidy and upright.
But he says, all these things I counted loss for the sake of Christ, verse 7.
All this was of no use to him, because it all related to an external life and an
external glory, and he was determined not to live in this external life, but to go
through the veil to have an inward life hidden with Christ in God.
And that's how he came into an experience of a true circumcision, where he went
through the veil and entered through and decided to lay hold of that
righteousness which comes from God.
And this is what he goes on to say in the succeeding verses, of how he found that
his own righteousness which came from the law was inadequate, and he desired
to have this righteousness which comes from God.
This external life alone didn't satisfy him.
If your external good testimony satisfies you, then you cannot enter into the
new covenant.
You will not desire a circumcision, but if you long for an inward pure life,
you will enter into that true circumcision of God's people.
We turn now to Philippians 3 and verse 6, where Paul says,
As to zeal a persecutor of the church, as to the righteousness which is in the
law, found blameless, but whatever things were gained to me, those I have
counted as loss for the sake of Christ.
More than that, I count all things to be loss in view of the surpassing value of
knowing Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I have suffered the loss of all
things, and count them but rubbish in order that I may gain Christ, and be
found in Him, not having a righteousness of my own derived from the law, but
that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which comes from God
on the basis of faith, that I may know Him in the power of His resurrection
and the fellowship of His sufferings, being conformed to His death, in
order that I may attain to the resurrection from among the dead.
Now how is it that someone whose righteousness, according to the law, was found
blameless, as he says in verse 6, was still dissatisfied?
Most people in the world are quite happy when they have a good external
testimony before men.
A good report from their fellow men is what most Christians also long for,
and this is the meaning of a righteousness which is blameless according to the law.
The law said, Thou shalt honor Thy father and mother, and keep the Sabbath day
holy, and don't take the name of the Lord in vain, and don't kill, don't steal,
don't bear false witness in things like this, everything relating to an
external life primarily.
And Paul kept all of these, and he was blameless concerning that external
righteousness of the law.
His life was upright externally.
Yet it says he was not satisfied.
Why was he not satisfied?
Because he found that he could not overcome covetousness and lust in his heart.
He says, for example, in Romans chapter 7, concerning the tenth
commandment.
Romans chapter 7, verse 7, What shall we say, then?
Is the law sin?
May it never be.
On the contrary, I would not have come to know sin except through the law, for I would not
have known about coveting or lust.
If the law had not said, You shall not covet, or You shall not lust.
That is the tenth commandment.
But sin taking opportunity through the commandment produced in me coveting of every kind, for
apart from the law sin is dead.
And he says how the law showed him his need, not in his external life.
He had not killed anyone, as far as the law was concerned.
He had not committed adultery or borne false witness.
But he found sin in his heart, sin in his flesh entering into his heart, and he found
himself powerless, because the flesh was so powerful to sin, so weak to do the will
of God.
And when he recognized this, he desired something more.
For most Christians, when they find sin in their thoughts and in their hearts, they are
not disturbed, provided they have a good testimony before men.
And that is why they never progress beyond a righteousness which is of the law, an external
righteousness which gives them a blameless testimony before men.
But Paul says here in verse 7, All this external testimony in men thinking that I am a very
upright righteous person, all this, he says in verse 7, I count it as loss.
For the sake of Christ.
What is the use of all this?
What is the use of men thinking that I am all right, if God doesn't think so?
And he says in verse 8, More than that, I count all things to be lost, not just the
things that were gained to him, his good testimony, and the reputation he had built
up for himself, and the honor he counted it all as loss.
And he says he counted everything as loss because of the surpassing value of knowing Christ
Jesus, my Lord.
The greatest thing Paul discovered was to know Jesus Christ.
Jesus said in John 17.3, This is life eternal, that they might know Thee the only true God,
and Jesus Christ whom Thou hast sent.
The whole basis of eternal life is in knowing God and in knowing Jesus Christ, not knowing
about Him or knowing the facts about Him, but knowing Him intimately in the Spirit.
The word knowing is a word used in the Old Testament to describe the husband-wife relationship
in the flesh, the two becoming one flesh.
Now in a somewhat of a similar way, in the Spirit, we are to know God and become one
with Him in our spirit.
We read in 1 Corinthians 6, 17, He who is joined to the Lord is one Spirit.
And this is what Paul desired, to know God in this way, to know Him intimately, and
to know Jesus Christ is Lord.
This is one of the privileges of the New Covenant.
We read in Hebrews 8, verses 9-12, All shall know Me, says the Lord, from the least to
the greatest of them.
Each one of us can come into that personal, intimate knowledge of God.
They shall not teach every man his neighbor, saying, Know the Lord, for all shall know
Me.
This is a New Covenant promise, because the veil has been rent.
One could not know God under the law, because he was blocked off by this veil called the
flesh.
But now that veil has been rent, Jesus has made a new and living way through the
flesh when He walked on earth and died on the cross.
Now we can enter into the Most Holy Place and know God and know the Lord Jesus.
And He says, Everything else is rubbish.
If I can gain Christ, if I know Him, and He says, I have actually, verse 8,
uncovered the loss of all things, all that reputation He had gotten, all that honor, and
all that accumulated knowledge that led Him astray and made Him think that Christianity
was a heresy, all that He gave up, and He counted it all as rubbish in order that
I may gain Christ.
Now how is it that He discovered that everything else was rubbish, apart from knowing Christ
and gaining Him and gaining His glory?
The word gain indicates that there is a price to be paid.
In 2 Thessalonians 2, verse 14, Paul says, It was for this that God called you through
our gospel, that you may gain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.
There is something to be gained, in other words, something that we have to pay a price for.
Forgiveness of sins and the baptism in the Holy Spirit are the free gifts of
God to all who will repent and to all who will turn from their sin and put their faith
in Christ.
But when it comes to gaining the glory of the Lord Jesus, as we read in 2 Thessalonians
2.14, or gaining Christ as it is written in Philippians 3.8, the word gain itself indicates
that there is a price to be paid.
There are things which are free and without price, but there are other things for which
we have to pay a price, for example, to be a disciple of the Lord Jesus.
Jesus said in Luke 14, verse 27-32, That we must count the costs, sit down first,
He said, and calculate the cost, and decide whether you want to be a disciple,
after having counted how much it is going to cost you.
And it is the same thing here.
Paul, when he encountered Jesus on the Damascus road, he went away for three years to Arabia.
We read in Galatians 1, and he sat down there and he counted the cost, and he decided that
everything that he had accumulated in his life that far, whether it was money, or reputation,
or honor, or success, or anything, or knowledge, it was all rubbish.
It was all rubbish, and he decided to throw it all off, that he might have that wealth
which is real wealth indeed, to know Christ and to gain Him.
Now the only people who can know the Lord Jesus in this intimate way and gain Christ
and come into that righteousness which comes from God and enter into that new covenant of
intimate relationship with God are those who are willing to follow in Paul's footsteps,
that is, particularly as mentioned in verse 8, to count all things as loss, and to suffer
the loss of all things, and to count it all as rubbish.
If there is anything upon this earth, whether it is wealth, or the honor of men, or any
pleasure, or any delight that we think is a gain, and that we yearn for, and that we
look for and long for, then we cannot enter into this glorious divine life that Paul entered
into.
The only way to enter into this life is by paying the price that Paul paid, and that
is to count everything earthly, whether it is honor, or wealth, or pleasure, as rubbish.
And then we can gain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.
And it is because people have not made this choice in these areas, that they still have
their mind set on something earthly, that they cannot know God in this way, and they
cannot come into the full glory of the new covenant.
We turn now to Philippians chapter 3 and verse 8.
More than that, I count all things to be loss in view of the surpassing value of knowing
Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and count them but
rubbish in order that I may gain Christ, and may be found in Him, not having a righteousness
of my own derived from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness
which comes from God, on the basis of faith, that I may know Him in the power of His resurrection
and the fellowship of His sufferings, being conformed to His death, in order that I may
attain to the resurrection from among the dead.
Now Paul says here that he counted everything as loss in order that he may know Christ,
verse 8, in order that he may gain Christ, verse 8, and, verse 9, be found in Him.
Now this is a phrase that is often found in Paul's writings, to be in Christ.
Now when we are found in Christ, one of the results of it, mentioned in verse 9, is, we
do not have a righteousness of our own derived from the law, but a righteousness which comes
through faith in Christ, the righteousness which comes from God, on the basis of faith.
Now we could ask ourselves this question, which righteousness is greater, that which
comes through our own efforts, in order to keep the law, or that which comes through faith,
which comes from God.
In other words, is it our own effort producing righteousness, which brings better life, or
is it the righteousness of God which is going to bring a better life?
The answer is clear.
It is obvious that the righteousness which comes from God should produce a far superior
life to the righteousness which comes through self-effort with an uncircumcised heart and
which produces merely the external blameless testimony that people who lived under the
old covenant and kept the law had.
In other words, the life that we can live today is as much superior to the life of old
covenant believers as the life of Jesus, superior to the life of Moses.
For Moses, he symbolized in his own life the height to which the law could take
a man.
Moses brought the gospel and the new covenant and demonstrated through his life where the
good news of the grace of God could take a man.
So there we have a contrast.
The old covenant was sealed with the blood of bulls and goats.
The new covenant is sealed with the blood of Jesus Christ.
And it is through that blood that we come into fellowship with God and have a righteousness
which comes from God which is as much superior to the righteousness of old covenant
believers as the blood of Jesus is to the blood of bulls and goats, as Jesus is superior
to Moses.
This is why Jesus said that although John the Baptist, Matthew 11, 11, was the greatest
person born until then, yet he who was least in the kingdom of God, who he who had really
entered into the new covenant, could attain to a far more glorious life, a far superior
life to that which anybody in the old covenant could have.
In other words, as we look at the old covenant saints and see the heights to which they
rose when you think of Abraham and the life he lived, Elijah, John the Baptist, Isaiah,
any of the great men of God in the Old Testament, the heights to which they attained, Joseph,
the purity which he had, Job and the patience that he had, we can say that those who enter
into the new covenant can attain a far superior life to that which anybody could enter into
under the old covenant.
And so where a person calls himself a Christian today and one who has accepted Jesus as his
Lord and finds that his own standard of life is inferior, less than that of old covenant
believers, he has to ask himself why.
It's obvious that he has not entered into the new covenant.
His life is a living proof of the fact that he has not entered into the new covenant,
for if he had entered into the new covenant, it would have lifted him to a higher plane
than that which was possible under the law.
So dear friend, if you find that Old Testament believers had a superior life to yours, then
it's obvious that you have not entered into the new covenant fully.
And the reason is that perhaps you consider something of this earth as still valuable.
Paul considered everything on earth as rubbish, and therefore he could press on into the new
covenant and be found in Christ not having a righteousness of his own which he produced
through self-effort, but a righteousness which came from God on the basis of faith, a righteousness
which was not merely external, for that is the righteousness of the law, but a righteousness
which was inward.
In the old covenant, the law was written externally on tables of stone.
Under the new covenant, we are told that the law is written inwardly in our hearts.
His laws are written on our mind and in our hearts.
In other words, we don't just keep the external law, but we keep it in our hearts.
What this means in practical terms is exactly what Jesus said in Matthew 5.20 and all the
following verses of the Sermon on the Mount.
When Jesus said in Matthew 5.20 that your righteousness must be superior and exceed
and surpass the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, what did he mean?
He meant was that our righteousness should be more than merely an external righteousness,
for the Pharisees had an external righteousness.
He said your righteousness must surpass that if you want to enter the kingdom of God,
because the kingdom of God is an inward thing.
It's the rule of God in every area of our life.
And Paul says here that he wanted that righteousness which was inward.
And Jesus went on to say in the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew 5.21, that the ancients only
demanded that you shouldn't murder, but I say to you, you shouldn't even hate, you
shouldn't be angry against your brother, you shouldn't hold your brother with contempt
or despise him, or call him a stupid idiot.
No, that was a superior righteousness to the old covenant righteousness.
He said the ancients demanded that you should not commit adultery, but I say to you that
you are not even to lust in your heart.
And this is how God leads us to be free from the law.
For if I am dealing with sin in the flesh, so that as soon as I am tempted I resist
temptation and keep my heart pure, pure from lust, pure from hatred, pure from anger and
bitterness and jealousy and contempt, the result will be that I do not need a law to
regulate my external life because I am dealing with these sins at a far deeper level.
This is how we are freed from the law.
